# Bento sync protocol (v1, with collections)

Server: `bento-sync` (Rust, `server/`), self-hosted behind nginx (`scripts/deploy-server.sh`).
Single user, single shared bearer token. All timestamps are Unix **milliseconds**.

## Note object

```json
{
  "id": "6F1C2D3E-....",          // UUID string, generated by the client
  "body": "# Title\n\nmarkdown…",  // full markdown text of the note
  "created_at": 1761000000000,
  "updated_at": 1761000123456,     // client clock at last local edit
  "deleted": false,                // tombstone; body is "" when deleted
  "seq": 42,                       // server-assigned, strictly increasing per change (absent in client puts)
  "device": "MacBook-Pro",         // device that made the last change
  "meta": {},                      // opaque JSON object for client extras (e.g. {"pinned":true}); max 4 KB
  "collection": "notes"            // which app the document belongs to (see Collections); default "notes"
}
```

`meta` keys used by the Notes client: `pinned` (bool), `pinOrder` (number, order within
pinned notes), `trashedAt` (ms; set when moved to Recently Deleted, purged after 60 days by
turning the note into a tombstone), `conflictOf` (id of the note this one is a
"conflicted copy" of: when a client's unsynced edit loses last-writer-wins to a
different text from another device and the two can't be merged, the client keeps its
losing text as a new note titled "‹title› (conflicted copy, ‹device›)" instead of
discarding it), `base` (written on Notes puts: `{"at": updated_at, "from": "<install
id>", "heads": {"<install id>": [updated_at, "<hash>"], ...}}`: `from` is the sending
install's random id (computer names can repeat; the id is tied to the Mac's hardware UUID, so
a database restored onto another Mac gets a new one); `retired` (optional) lists ids its
sender found in use by two Macs at once; `heads`, absent when the sender doesn't
know them, says for each install the newest version of that install's text this version
contains, as its `updated_at` and the hex FNV-1a hash of its UTF-8 body, like a version
vector, at most 16 (the most recently edited); only valid while `at` equals the note's
`updated_at`, so a client that edits the note without rewriting `base` invalidates it;
see Client behaviour). Unknown keys must be preserved.

`body` max size 1 MB. The title is derived by clients (first non-empty line that isn't an
image, markdown stripped); the server never parses `body` (except `gc-blobs`, see Images).

## Images

Images aren't in the note text. Each is a **blob**, stored once on the server under the
lowercase hex SHA-256 of its bytes, and the note refers to it with a Markdown image on a
line of its own:

```markdown
![alt text](bento-image:9f86d081884c7d659a2feaa0c55ad015a3bf4f1b2b0b822cd15d6c15b0f00a08)
```

* **Format.** `bento-image:` then 64 lowercase hex digits. The alt text is optional
  (`![](…)`), may not contain `]`, and isn't shown. Only a line that is nothing but one
  such image (spaces around it allowed), outside a fenced code block, is an image;
  anywhere else the text is just text. A client that doesn't know images shows the line as it is.
* **Blobs** are PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP or HEIC/HEIF, at most 10 MB. Clients convert other
  formats (TIFF, BMP…) to PNG, or JPEG for photos, and scale down anything larger before
  hashing. A blob never changes, so it can be cached for good. Clients show images
  upright per their EXIF orientation (the bytes are kept as they are).
* **Inserting.** Write the blob to the local cache, insert the line, upload it (one at a
  time; the server serves blob requests one by one) with
  `PUT /v1/blobs/<hash>` (raw bytes), retrying (with a backoff while connected, and on
  every reconnect) until the server has it, and keep it pending across restarts. Clients only upload to a server whose `/v1/health` says
  `"blobs": true`. The note itself syncs as usual and doesn't wait for the upload.
* **Server reset.** On every connect a client asks `POST /v1/blobs/missing` which of the
  images in its cache the server lacks (in batches) and uploads those: a server restored
  from a backup, or a new one, gets back the images uploaded since (only those it lacks
  are sent). A client also asks right away when it sees the server's seq go backwards.
* **Showing.** A blob that isn't cached is fetched with `GET /v1/blobs/<hash>`. A 404
  (the sending device hasn't uploaded it yet) shows a placeholder and is retried later:
  when the note is shown again or sync reconnects.
* **Removing** an image is removing its line. The server keeps blobs no document refers
  to until an admin runs `bento-sync gc-blobs` (only blobs last uploaded over 30 days ago,
  so an upload whose note hasn't arrived yet is safe; a trashed note's text still refers to
  its images).

## Collections

One server stores documents for several apps. Every document belongs to exactly one
**collection**: `notes` (the Notes module), `todos` (the Todo module) or `voice`
(dictation's dictionary and settings). Names match `[a-z][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}`; the server
doesn't keep a fixed list.

* `id`s are unique across all collections. A put whose id already exists in a
  different collection is refused (REST 409 `{"error":…}`, WebSocket `error` with the id).
* `seq` is still one global counter, so a client sees gaps in the seqs of its own
  collection. That is expected; `since` filters use the global seq.
* Everything that predates collections, and every request that doesn't name one, is
  `notes`. Clients built before collections keep working unchanged and never see
  other collections' documents.
* Documents sent by the server always carry `"collection"`.
* Clients of any collection other than `notes` must check `/v1/health` for
  `"collections": true` before syncing: an older server ignores `collections` and would
  store their documents as notes.

## Todo documents (`collection: "todos"`)

The server treats them like any document (opaque `body`, LWW on `updated_at`). The
Todo client stores one task or project per document; `body` is a JSON object:

```json
{
  "type": "task",                       // "task" | "project"
  "fields": {
    "title": "Buy milk",
    "description": "",
    "project": "8E1F…" ,                // project document id; null = Inbox
    "labels": ["errands"],              // label names (labels have no documents)
    "priority": 1,                      // 1 = p1 (highest) … 4 = p4 (default, none)
    "due": {"date": "2026-10-23", "time": "17:00"},  // floating local date, optional "HH:mm"; null = no date
    "completed_at": null,               // ms when completed; null = open
    "order": 1024.0                     // position within its project (fractional)
  },
  "clocks": {"title": 1761000123456, "due": 1761000200000}   // per-field last change (ms)
}
```

Project `fields`: `name`, `color` (name from the client palette), `order`, `archived` (bool).
Fields absent from `fields` take their defaults; unknown fields and types must be preserved.

**Merge.** Two devices editing different fields of the same task must both win, so
clients merge field by field: for each field the value with the larger clock wins
(ties: the value whose canonical JSON sorts higher), and the document's `updated_at`
is the largest clock. When a remote version arrives for a task with unsent local
changes, the client merges, keeps the result dirty and puts it with
`updated_at = max(clocks) + 1` if that differs from what the server has; a rejected put is
handled the same way with the stored winner. A tombstone (`deleted:true`) wins
over every field change older than its `updated_at`; a field change made after it
resurrects the task (its put carries the full body).

## Voice documents (`collection: "voice"`)

Dictation's personal dictionary and cleanup settings, shared by every Mac and the
Android app. The body format and the merge, tie-break and tombstone rules are the
todo documents' (`{"type", "fields", "clocks"}`, merged field by field). Unknown
fields and unknown types are stored and preserved untouched, and never shown.

`type: "entry"`, one dictionary entry. The id is the entry's UUID string (the Mac
writes `UUID().uuidString`, upper case; compare ids as UUIDs).

```json
{
  "type": "entry",
  "fields": {
    "term": "Kubernetes",               // the right spelling, 1–60 characters after trimming
    "misspelling": "cooper netties",    // what the recogniser tends to write; null = none
    "starred": false,                   // starred terms go first in the prompt
    "created_at": 1761000000000         // ms; absent: the document's created_at
  },
  "clocks": {"term": 1761000000000, "misspelling": 1761000000000, "starred": 1761000200000, "created_at": 1761000000000}
}
```

`type: "settings"`, a singleton with the id `"voice-settings"`. Fields, named like the
Mac's settings keys: `customInstructions` (string, default `""`),
`customInstructionsEnabled` (bool, default `false`) and `cleanupEnabled` (bool, default
`true`, the cleanup pass's master switch). A missing field, or one of the wrong type,
means the default.

`type: "mode"`, the Android app's dictation profiles: fields `name`, `prompt`, `order`,
`language` and `cleanup`. Android only; the Mac keeps them as they are.

**First sync.** A client that has never synced uploads what it has, stamped so it never
overrides an edit made while syncing: a new entry document's field clocks are its
`created_at`, and a setting it had before it started syncing gets clock `1` when no
document has a clock for that field yet (settings still at their defaults aren't sent).
Edits made while syncing get the current time as usual. So the dictionaries of several devices
union by id, a stale copy of an entry deleted elsewhere stays deleted (its clocks are
older than the tombstone), and the settings document merges per field; two never-synced
values of one setting tie, and the canonical-JSON tie-break picks one.

**One term, several entries.** Two devices can add the same term (ignoring case) under
different ids. Both documents stay. Clients show one entry for them: the one with the
smaller `created_at` (then the smaller id), starred if any of them is, with the first
misspelling any of them has, in the same order. An edit to that entry is written to
every document behind it (`created_at` only to its own), and removing it deletes them
all.

## Auth

Every request carries `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. (`?token=<token>` is also accepted for manual testing.)
Wrong/missing token → HTTP 401 (WebSocket upgrade refused with 401).

## REST

| Method | Path | Body | Response |
|---|---|---|---|
| GET | `/v1/health` | – | `{"ok":true,"seq":<latest seq>,"collections":true,"blobs":true}` (no auth; `collections` and `blobs` only on servers that have them) |
| GET | `/v1/notes?since=<seq>` | – | `{"notes":[Note…],"seq":<latest seq>}` – all notes (incl. tombstones) with `seq > since`, ascending |
| PUT | `/v1/notes/<id>` | Note (no `seq`) | `{"note":Note,"accepted":true}` or `{"note":<stored Note>,"accepted":false}` |
| DELETE | `/v1/notes/<id>?updated_at=<ms>` | – | same as PUT with `deleted:true, body:""` |
| GET | `/v1/c/<collection>?since=<seq>` | – | `{"docs":[Doc…],"seq":<latest seq>}` – like `/v1/notes`, for any collection |
| PUT | `/v1/c/<collection>/<id>` | Doc (no `seq`) | `{"doc":Doc,"accepted":bool}` |
| DELETE | `/v1/c/<collection>/<id>?updated_at=<ms>` | – | same as PUT with `deleted:true, body:""` |
| PUT | `/v1/blobs/<hash>` | image bytes | `{"hash":…,"type":"image/png","size":<bytes>,"created":bool}`; 400 when `hash` isn't the SHA-256 of the body, 413 over 10 MB, 415 when it isn't an image. Idempotent |
| POST | `/v1/blobs/missing` | `{"hashes":[…]}` (at most 2000) | `{"missing":[…]}`: those the server doesn't have |
| GET | `/v1/blobs/<hash>` | – | the bytes, `Content-Type` from them, `Cache-Control: immutable`; 404 when the server doesn't have it (`HEAD` works too) |

`/v1/notes…` is `/v1/c/notes…` with the original response keys (`notes`, `note`). A
`collection` in a PUT body must match the path (400 otherwise).

## WebSocket: `GET /v1/sync` (upgrade)

Client → server:

```json
{"type":"hello","since":<last seq the client has applied>,"device":"MacBook-Pro","collections":["todos"]}
{"type":"put","note":{…Note without seq…}}
{"type":"ping"}
```

Server → client:

```json
{"type":"snapshot","notes":[…],"seq":<latest>}         // reply to hello: everything with seq > since
{"type":"ack","id":"…","seq":43,"accepted":true}       // reply to the sender's put
{"type":"note","note":{…}}                              // a change made by another connection, or the
                                                        // stored winner when the sender's put was rejected
{"type":"pong"}
{"type":"error","message":"…"}
```

Server sends a WebSocket ping frame every 30 s; clients may also send `{"type":"ping"}`.

`collections` (optional, default `["notes"]`, 1–8 names) chooses what the connection
receives: the snapshot and `note` broadcasts only contain documents of those
collections. A put's collection is `note.collection`, defaulting to the connection's
first collection. Puts to a collection the connection didn't subscribe to are acked but
never echoed back to it (not even the stored winner of a rejected put).

## Conflict rule (last writer wins)

A put for an existing id is **accepted** iff `put.updated_at >= stored.updated_at`
(ties: accepted). Accepted puts get `seq = ++global_seq`, are stored, acked to the
sender and broadcast as `note` to every other connection. A rejected put is acked
with `accepted:false` and the stored note is sent back to the sender as `note`
so it can adopt it. `created_at` is kept from the first version.

## Client behaviour (reference: Notes module; Todo and voice follow it with field merges)

- Keep notes in a local SQLite DB; the app works fully offline.
- Track `last_seq` (highest applied server seq) and a per-note `dirty` flag.
- Debounce local edits (~400 ms) then send `put`; clear `dirty` on `ack accepted` for
  that id if the note was not edited again meanwhile.
- On (re)connect: `hello{since:last_seq}`, apply snapshot, then re-send all dirty notes.
- Applying a remote note (Notes) that carries `meta.base`, when the local text's heads
  are known: exactly one of two clients with concurrent versions merges them, the one
  whose version the server no longer has. A remote version made without our latest put
  that arrives while that put is in flight waits for its ack: stored after ours, we
  merge onto it; stored before ours (ours overwrote it) or our put refused (the winner
  follows), it is dropped, as its sender merges. Otherwise the local text is merged
  three-way with the remote one from a known text whose heads are exactly what both
  contain (the element-wise minimum); both sides' changes are applied when they don't
  touch the same text, the result is stored dirty with a newer `updated_at` and sent,
  and the other client takes it as a fast-forward. Two clients merging the same pair of
  versions get the same text.
- No such text is known (heads disagree, three or more clients edited at the same
  moment, or the history is gone), or the changes overlap: last-writer-wins as below,
  and a synced local text the remote one overwrote is kept as a conflicted copy.
- Meta (pin, trash…) is merged key by key against the base text's meta: a key changed
  locally keeps the local value.
- A remote version that waits for an ack holds `last_seq` just below its seq, so after a
  crash the next hello fetches it again.
- Two Macs using one install id (a copied database while the old Mac still syncs: a
  version arrives with our id and another computer name, or with our id in `retired`):
  pick a new id, retire the old one, forget all heads. Heads naming a retired id aren't
  trusted (last-writer-wins with conflicted copies until new history arrives).
- A version from a client that sends `from` but no heads (its history is gone) that would
  remove text from a synced local note whose heads are known keeps the local text as a
  conflicted copy first (without heads on either side, e.g. right after upgrading, it's an
  ordinary edit). Identical conflicted copies of one note (same `conflictOf` and body)
  are kept once: the one with the smaller id stays, the other becomes a tombstone.
- Heads are stored with each note, tagged with the hash of the body they describe (an
  older build that edits the note leaves them behind; they're dropped on load). The
  texts merges start from are kept in memory only,
  so right after a relaunch a concurrent edit falls back to last-writer-wins, keeping
  the local text as a conflicted copy when the heads show the remote one lacks it. A
  put without heads counts as the start of a note's history.
- Otherwise (no `meta.base`, e.g. an older client, or local heads unknown): if the local
  copy is not dirty → overwrite. If dirty and remote
  `updated_at` is newer → adopt remote (LWW) and keep the local text as a conflicted
  copy. Otherwise keep local and (re)send it.
- An open note takes remote text like Google Docs: only the changed stretches are
  replaced, the selection moves with the text around it (text inserted right at a caret
  goes after it), and the line at the top of the view stays there.
- Reconnect with exponential backoff (1 s … 60 s). If WebSocket upgrade keeps failing
  (e.g. a corporate proxy), fall back to REST polling `GET /v1/notes?since=` every 10 s
  and `PUT` for writes.

## Config (client)

Config section `notes.sync` in `~/.config/bento/config.json` (`todo.sync` for Todo). Sync is
off and there is no server by default:

```json
"sync": { "enabled": true, "server": "https://sync.example.com", "tokenFile": "~/.config/bento/sync-token" }
```

The token file contains only the token (mode 600) and is never written into config.json.
The `voice` collection uses `notes.sync`, while a voice module runs and
`dictation.syncDictionary` (Settings → Dictation → Sync dictionary and instructions) isn't
`false`.

## Pairing link (Android)

Settings → Notes or Todo → Pair Android Phone… shows this as a QR code, and Copy Link
copies it:

```
bento://pair?v=1&server=<server>&token=<token>&name=<computer name>[&gemini=<Gemini API key>]
```

Every value is percent-encoded except the RFC 3986 unreserved characters
(`A–Z a–z 0–9 - . _ ~`), so `+` is `%2B` and a space is `%20`. `server` is the base URL as
clients use it: `https://` added when the config leaves out the scheme, no trailing
slash. It comes from `notes.sync` when that names a server, else `todo.sync` (one that is
switched on first), and `token` from its token file. `gemini` is present only when the
Mac has a key and the user ticks Include Gemini API key. `v` is the link's version.
